claims.claim: LEF1 was only slightly overexpressed in the pleurodont SDL with a pleurodont/acrodont fold change of 2.2.
claims.source: Furthermore, apart from LEF1 that was only slightly overexpressed in the pleurodont SDL (pleurodont/acrodont fold change of 2.2), many homeotic transcriptional regulators (BARX1, ALX1/ALX4, SIX3, DLX2) and members of classical signaling pathways (BMP7, WNT11, FGF7) were highly differentially expressed between the two dentition types.
claims.evidence: Obtained from RNA sequencing analysis.

claims.claim: Many homeotic transcriptional regulators (BARX1, ALX1/ALX4, SIX3, DLX2) were highly differentially expressed between pleurodont and acrodont dentition types.
claims.source: Furthermore, apart from LEF1 that was only slightly overexpressed in the pleurodont SDL (pleurodont/acrodont fold change of 2.2), many homeotic transcriptional regulators (BARX1, ALX1/ALX4, SIX3, DLX2) and members of classical signaling pathways (BMP7, WNT11, FGF7) were highly differentially expressed between the two dentition types.
claims.evidence: Obtained from RNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: More than 45% of differentially regulated genes belong to the GO category 'developmental process'.

claims.evidence: Obtained from GO analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The list of developmental genes revealed only a partial overlap (18%) with genes already known to be expressed in vertebrate dental tissues.
claims.source: Surprisingly, however, our list of developmental genes revealed only a partial overlap (18%) with genes already known to be expressed in vertebrate dental tissues (Figure 5B), indicating that regulation of the SDL in polyphyodont dentitions involves many genes and signaling pathways still uncharacterized and/or non-expressed in the monophyodont mouse dentition.
claims.evidence: Obtained from comparison of transcriptome data with existing dental gene databases shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Regulation of the SDL in polyphyodont dentitions involves many genes and signaling pathways still uncharacterized and/or non-expressed in the monophyodont mouse dentition.
claims.source: Surprisingly, however, our list of developmental genes revealed only a partial overlap (18%) with genes already known to be expressed in vertebrate dental tissues (Figure 5B), indicating that regulation of the SDL in polyphyodont dentitions involves many genes and signaling pathways still uncharacterized and/or non-expressed in the monophyodont mouse dentition.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the low overlap between identified genes and known dental genes.

claims.claim: SIX3 and ISL1 were significantly upregulated in the pleurodont epithelium.

claims.claim: FOXI1 and BARX1 were downregulated in the pleurodont mesenchyme.
claims.source: Of the selected genes, SIX3 and ISL1 were significantly upregulated in the pleurodont epithelium, FOXI1 and BARX1 were downregulated in the pleurodont mesenchyme, and ALX1 was significantly enriched in both pleurodont epithelial and mesenchymal tissues (Figure 5A,C).
claims.evidence: Confirmed through qPCR shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: ALX1 was significantly enriched in both pleurodont epithelial and mesenchymal tissues.
claims.source: Of the selected genes, SIX3 and ISL1 were significantly upregulated in the pleurodont epithelium, FOXI1 and BARX1 were downregulated in the pleurodont mesenchyme, and ALX1 was significantly enriched in both pleurodont epithelial and mesenchymal tissues (Figure 5A,C).
claims.evidence: Confirmed through qPCR shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The relatively higher expression of ALX1 and SIX3 in pleurodont versus acrodont tissues was apparent in all stages tested by ISH.

claims.claim: Differential ISL1 expression between the dentition types was only apparent at late tooth developmental stages.

claims.claim: The expression pattern of ISL1 and SIX3 was largely restricted to the SDL postnatally in both types of teeth.
claims.source: As already revealed by our transcriptomic data, the expression pattern of ISL1 and SIX3 was largely restricted to the SDL postnatally in both types of teeth, while being detected in both epithelium and dental papilla mesenchyme at embryonic dental stages.
claims.evidence: Observed through ISH analysis shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: ALX1 was confined to the developing pleurodont mesenchymes at all embryonic stages.
claims.source: In contrast, ALX1 was confined to the developing pleurodont mesenchymes at all embryonic stages, but was later detected both in the pleurodont SDL and surrounding mesenchyme of postnatal teeth, thus supporting our RNA sequencing results and indicating dynamic expression pattern during tooth development and SDL patterning.
claims.evidence: Observed through ISH analysis shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: ALX1 was detected both in the pleurodont SDL and surrounding mesenchyme of postnatal teeth.
claims.source: In contrast, ALX1 was confined to the developing pleurodont mesenchymes at all embryonic stages, but was later detected both in the pleurodont SDL and surrounding mesenchyme of postnatal teeth, thus supporting our RNA sequencing results and indicating dynamic expression pattern during tooth development and SDL patterning.
claims.evidence: Observed through ISH analysis shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The early degradation of the SDL is not the only mechanism restricting vertebrate tooth replacement.
claims.source: As already shown in non-teleost polyphyodont species, our findings first confirm the critical importance of both DL and SDL structures in tooth renewal. However, in contrast to a previous hypothesis (Buchtová et al., 2012; Dosedělová et al., 2015), the early degradation of the SDL is not the only mechanism restricting vertebrate tooth replacement.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that bearded dragon acrodont SDL persists without tooth replacement.

claims.claim: Bearded dragons maintain a proliferative epithelial SDL structure even in non-replacing teeth.
claims.source: Indeed, bearded dragons maintain a proliferative epithelial SDL structure even in non-replacing teeth, indicating that the SDL maintenance is independent of and not strictly associated with tooth renewal.
claims.evidence: Observed through PCNA IHC and BrdU incorporation in acrodont teeth.

claims.claim: The bearded dragon posterior dentition might represent an intermediary stage between polyphyodonty and complete monophyodonty, at least at the cellular level.
claims.source: The bearded dragon posterior dentition might thus represent an intermediary stage between polyphyodonty and complete monophyodonty, at least at the cellular level.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation of SDL persistence in acrodont teeth.

claims.claim: The implantation mode in most agamids is similar to intermediate pleurodont-acrodont dentition patterns observed in extinct acrodont iguanian lizards.
claims.source: In favor of that, and in contrast to chameleons, the implantation mode in most agamids is similar to intermediate pleurodont-acrodont dentition patterns observed in extinct acrodont iguanian lizards (Averianov et al., 1996; Simões et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The posterior tooth phenotype in bearded dragons might result from pleurodont to acrodont remodeling changes through ontogeny.
claims.source: Haridy even recently proposed that the posterior tooth phenotype in bearded dragons might result from pleurodont to acrodont remodeling changes through ontogeny (Haridy, 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: No clear morphological variations were observed in the two types of developing teeth, except for the length of the embryonic primary DL.
claims.source: The latter hypothesis is coherent with our developmental data, as no clear morphological variations were observed in the two types of developing teeth, except for the length of the embryonic primary DL.
claims.evidence: Observed through histological analysis of embryonic teeth.

claims.claim: The difference in developing DL length might be linked to the delayed initiation of pleurodont teeth.
claims.source: The origin of such difference in the developing DL is unclear but might be linked to the delayed initiation of pleurodont teeth, when compared to acrodont teeth, which would extend the timing of DL proliferation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observed developmental delay and DL length difference.

claims.claim: Differential directional SDL growth likely constitutes a key process to accommodate the replacement tooth.
claims.source: This differential directional SDL growth likely constitutes a key process to accommodate the replacement tooth, and was accompanied by an asymmetric expression pattern of conserved dental genes such as LEF1 and PITX2, but also of proliferation, towards the pleurodont SDL tip.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observed differences in SDL growth and gene expression patterns.

claims.claim: Focal localization of LEF1 expression and/or Wnt signaling activity was already noticed in the squamate SDL, alligator DL bulge, shark SDL, and ferret SDL.
claims.source: Interestingly, focal localization of LEF1 expression and/or Wnt signaling activity was already noticed in the squamate SDL (Handrigan et al., 2010; Gaete and Tucker, 2013), alligator DL bulge (Wu et al., 2013), shark SDL (Rasch et al., 2016), and ferret SDL (Jussila et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: A large number of yet uncharacterized developmental genes and signaling pathways are likely associated with SDL outgrowth and/or induction.
claims.source: However, our large-scale transcriptomic analysis now indicates that a large number of yet uncharacterized developmental genes and signaling pathways are, in fact, likely associated with SDL outgrowth and/or induction.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the transcriptomic analysis showing many new developmental genes.

claims.claim: The overall conserved expression levels of Wnt signaling members in the comparative pleurodont-acrodont transcriptome analysis suggest that this pathway might primarily regulate SDL growth rather than directly induce tooth replacement.
claims.source: Along this line, the overall conserved expression levels of Wnt signaling members in our comparative pleurodont-acrodont transcriptome analysis suggest that this conserved pathway might primarily regulate SDL growth, a process maintained in bearded dragon acrodont dentition, rather than directly induce tooth replacement.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the transcriptomic data showing similar Wnt expression levels.

claims.claim: Separate processes regulate SDL growth and initiation of replacement teeth.
claims.source: This hypothesis is consistent with our observations that separate processes regulate SDL growth and initiation of replacement teeth, further indicating that SDL maintenance is not causatively associated with tooth replacement.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that acrodont SDL grows without initiating replacement.

claims.claim: ALX1 is a regulator of cartilage and craniofacial development in vertebrates.
claims.source: For example, ALX1, a regulator of cartilage and craniofacial development in vertebrates (Zhao et al., 1993; Zhao et al., 1996; Dee et al., 2013), was one of the most highly upregulated genes in both pleurodont SDL and mesenchymal tissues, and it is likely that the severe and relatively early craniofacial phenotypes of ALX1 mutations (frontonasal dysplasia) before initiation of odontogenesis have hampered identification of this gene as a regulator of tooth development and/or replacement in mammals.

results.result: The bearded dragon possesses a unique heterodont dentition with both polyphyodont pleurodont teeth anteriorly (3 on premaxilla, 2 on dentary) and monophyodont acrodont teeth posteriorly (7 per jaw quadrant), with a continuous dental lamina (DL) that is shorter at acrodont positions and in interdental regions compared to pleurodont regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C20-C24 are directly supported by micro-CT imaging (Figure 1A-D) and PTA-stained CT scans showing the morphological features of the dentition. The observations are clearly documented with appropriate imaging techniques and are consistent with the stated tooth counts and DL morphology.

results.result: Acrodont tooth development begins at 15 dpo with vestigial teeth that abort prematurely, followed by functional teeth developing from a primary DL. A small SDL emerges and continues growing until hatching and postnatally. Pleurodont teeth show delayed initiation (40 dpo), an elongated primary DL, and differential SDL directional growth (lingual for pleurodont, downward for acrodont).
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C32 are well-supported by histological sections (Figure 1E-P) showing developmental stages and timing. The observations of vestigial teeth, SDL persistence, developmental delay, and directional growth differences are documented with appropriate histological evidence and are consistent with cited literature.

results.result: Expression patterns of conserved dental genes (SHH, PITX2, NOTCH1, LEF1) in bearded dragon are comparable to other polyphyodont species. PITX2 marks the primary DL and SDL, SHH localizes to inner enamel epithelium but not SDL, NOTCH1 is in epithelial compartment and OE, and LEF1 shows condensed expression in primary DL and SDL tip. All tested genes showed similar patterns in both acrodont and pleurodont embryonic teeth.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C40 are supported by ISH data (Figure 2A) showing gene expression patterns at multiple developmental stages. The patterns are consistent with previous literature citations and show appropriate spatial localization. The similarity between acrodont and pleurodont embryonic teeth is documented.

results.result: A highly proliferative SDL persists in both acrodont and pleurodont teeth at juvenile and adult stages without signs of deterioration or increased apoptosis in acrodont SDL. However, pleurodont SDL shows oral-aboral and labial-lingual asymmetry in PCNA, LEF1, and PITX2 expression, while acrodont SDL shows scattered patterns. This represents the first example of long-term SDL maintenance in non-polyphyodont dentition, suggesting SDL maintenance is independent of tooth replacement.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C49 are supported by PCNA IHC, BrdU incorporation, TUNEL assays, and ISH/IHC data (Figure 2B,C). The persistence of SDL without replacement in acrodont teeth is well-documented, and the asymmetry differences between tooth types are clearly shown. The novelty claim (C47) is appropriately qualified with 'to our knowledge.'

results.result: BrdU pulse-chase experiments reveal that at day 0, most PCNA+ cells are BrdU+, dropping dramatically by day 28. At day 58, BrdU+PCNA+ label-retaining cells (LRCs) in pleurodont teeth are concentrated in two distinct regions: the oral epithelium (OE) and deep dental lamina (DDL), with the DDL and OE representing ~75% of all LRCs. Acrodont teeth show more equal LRC distribution and reduced DDL proliferation. The high DDL proliferation in pleurodont teeth may trigger directional SDL growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C59 are supported by double IHC for PCNA and BrdU (Figure 3A) with quantification (Figure 3C,D). The pulse-chase methodology is appropriate with multiple time points (0, 28, 58 days) and biological replicates (n=3-4). The spatial distribution analysis across four epithelial subdivisions provides clear evidence for the dual LRC populations in pleurodont teeth.

results.result: Stem/progenitor marker analysis reveals that in pleurodont teeth, SOX2/LGR5/IGFBP5 are co-expressed in the DDL LRC site while only SOX2 is expressed in the OE LRC site. In acrodont teeth, SOX2 is co-expressed in OE LRCs but no LGR5, IGFBP5, or SOX2 expression is detected in scattered BrdU+ cells of acrodont DL. This indicates separate putative dental epithelial stem/progenitor populations: one pleurodont-specific DDL population and one shared pleurodont/acrodont OE population.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C66 are supported by IHC and ISH combined with BrdU detection (Figure 3E,F). The co-localization studies clearly demonstrate differential marker expression between pleurodont and acrodont teeth, and between DDL and OE regions. The comparison with leopard gecko and catshark is appropriately cited.

results.result: DiI cell tracking experiments demonstrate that cells labeled in the OE migrate to the DL (day 7) and SDL (day 14) and contribute to replacement teeth in pleurodont dentition. Similar migration occurs in acrodont teeth despite lack of replacement. Ex vivo imaging confirms the migratory pathway from OE to SDL. OE removal experiments show that disruption of the OE leads to significant decrease in proliferating DL/SDL cells and some DL/SDL degeneration, confirming the regulatory role of OE on DL/SDL growth and tooth replacement.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C73 are supported by in vivo DiI labeling (Figure 4A), ex vivo culture imaging (Figure 4B), and OE removal experiments with quantification (Figure 4C,D). The cell tracking provides direct evidence of migration, and the functional perturbation experiment (OE removal) with statistical significance (p<0.05, n=4) demonstrates the regulatory role of the OE.

results.result: RNA sequencing analysis identified 206 differentially expressed genes in SDL and 368 in dental mesenchyme between pleurodont and acrodont teeth (FDR<0.05). Candidate genes PITX2, LEF1, and SOX2 were retrieved, validating the approach. LEF1 showed modest overexpression (2.2-fold), while many homeotic transcriptional regulators (BARX1, ALX1/ALX4, SIX3, DLX2) and signaling pathway members were highly differentially expressed. Over 45% of differentially regulated genes belong to 'developmental process' GO category, but only 18% overlap with known vertebrate dental genes, indicating many uncharacterized genes are involved in SDL regulation in polyphyodont dentitions.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C82 are supported by RNA-seq data with appropriate statistical analysis (FDR correction, n=3 biological replicates per group) and visualization (Figure 5A). The GO analysis (Figure 5B) and comparison with existing dental gene databases provide strong evidence for the novelty of identified genes. The low overlap (18%) with known dental genes is a significant finding.

results.result: qPCR validation confirmed differential expression of selected genes: SIX3 and ISL1 were significantly upregulated in pleurodont epithelium, FOXI1 and BARX1 were downregulated in pleurodont mesenchyme, and ALX1 was enriched in both pleurodont epithelial and mesenchymal tissues. ISH analysis showed that ALX1 and SIX3 higher expression in pleurodont tissues was apparent at all stages tested, while differential ISL1 expression was only apparent at late developmental stages. ALX1 was confined to pleurodont mesenchyme embryonically but later detected in both SDL and surrounding mesenchyme postnatally.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C90 are supported by qPCR with statistical analysis (Figure 5C, n=3, p-values indicated) and ISH at multiple developmental stages (Figure 6). The validation of RNA-seq results by independent method (qPCR) strengthens the findings. The dynamic expression patterns across developmental stages are well-documented.

results.result: The early degradation of SDL is not the only mechanism restricting vertebrate tooth replacement. Bearded dragons maintain a proliferative epithelial SDL structure even in non-replacing acrodont teeth, representing the first example of long-term SDL maintenance in non-polyphyodont dentition. This indicates that SDL maintenance is independent of and not causally related to tooth renewal.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 and related claims C46-C48 are supported by the observation of SDL persistence in acrodont teeth without tooth replacement (Figure 2B,C). This challenges previous hypotheses and is appropriately qualified with 'to our knowledge' for the novelty claim. The inference that SDL maintenance is independent of tooth replacement is logical given the data.

results.result: The bearded dragon posterior dentition might represent an intermediary stage between polyphyodonty and complete monophyodonty at the cellular level. The implantation mode in agamids is similar to intermediate pleurodont-acrodont patterns in extinct acrodont iguanian lizards. No clear morphological variations were observed between developing tooth types except for primary DL length, which might be linked to delayed pleurodont tooth initiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C97 are supported by developmental observations and appropriately cited literature (C94, C95). The interpretation of bearded dragon as an intermediate stage is reasonable given the SDL persistence data. However, C97 is speculative ('might be linked') and appropriately qualified as such in the text.

results.result: Differential directional SDL growth likely constitutes a key process to accommodate replacement teeth and is accompanied by asymmetric expression of conserved dental genes (LEF1, PITX2) and proliferation toward the pleurodont SDL tip. While focal LEF1/Wnt signaling was previously noted in other species, transcriptomic analysis indicates many uncharacterized developmental genes and signaling pathways are associated with SDL outgrowth/induction. Conserved Wnt expression levels suggest this pathway primarily regulates SDL growth rather than directly inducing tooth replacement, indicating separate processes regulate SDL growth and initiation of replacement teeth.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C102 are supported by the combination of morphological observations, gene expression patterns (Figure 2), and transcriptomic data (Figure 5). The inference about Wnt pathway function (C101) is reasonable given the conserved expression levels between tooth types. The conclusion about separate processes (C102) is logical given that acrodont SDL grows without initiating replacement.

results.result: Among newly identified genes, ALX1 (a regulator of cartilage and craniofacial development) was one of the most highly upregulated genes in both pleurodont SDL and mesenchymal tissues. SIX3 plays crucial roles in vertebrate sensory system development but has not been detected in developing mouse dentition. ISL1 is selectively expressed in mouse incisor dental epithelium but absent from molar epithelium, though this patterning has not been linked with tooth growth or replacement in previous vertebrate studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C107 are supported by transcriptomic data (C104) and appropriately cited literature for gene functions (C103, C105, C107). The citations support the known roles of these genes in other systems and their absence or limited characterization in dental contexts, highlighting the novelty of their identification in this study.

results.result: The identification of bearded dragon slow-cycling LRCs co-expressing stem/progenitor markers provides further evidence of the importance of epithelial stem/progenitor cell populations in regulating tooth renewal. The mechanism differs from leopard gecko by having two separate sources of putative stem/progenitor cells in the DL and OE. Migration from SOX2+ LRCs at the DL/OE junction contributes to proliferative growth of DL and SDL structures in both tooth types. This strategy closely parallels sharks with a similar LRC population at the taste/tooth junction.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C111 are supported by BrdU pulse-chase data (Figure 3), marker expression analysis, and DiI labeling experiments (Figure 4). The comparison with leopard gecko and shark is appropriately cited and illustrated in Figure 7. The dual stem/progenitor population represents a novel finding that expands understanding of vertebrate dental regenerative strategies.

results.result: SOX2+ OE cells of bearded dragons could be bipotent, contributing to both taste and dental lineages, as SOX2 is a conserved marker of dental progenitors and taste bud/non-gustatory epithelial fate. The OE contains heterogeneous cell populations including self-renewing epithelial progenitors and taste buds near the DL. However, anatomical studies show heterogeneity in taste bud presence/location in lizards and snakes, and it is unclear if the OE LRC population exists in other reptiles. The OE LRC population might be linked to specific tooth replacement rates/strategies in squamates.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C117 are largely speculative. C112 is explicitly speculative ('tempting to speculate'), C116 acknowledges uncertainty ('still unclear'), and C117 is hypothetical ('might be'). While C113-C115 are supported by citations and histological observations (Figure 3A), the broader implications about bipotency and conservation across species lack direct experimental evidence in this study.

results.result: Replacement of pleurodont teeth in agamid lizards is relatively slow and based on a 'one-for-one' strategy (single replacement tooth per position), whereas many squamates exhibit 'many-for-one' replacement (multiple replacement teeth per position). Conservation of only one stem/progenitor cell population in the DL might constitute a more efficient positioning strategy for generating multiple tooth generations. The bearded dragon pleurodont DL LRC population shows striking similarities with leopard gecko in location (beside lingually protruding SDL in DDL) and stem/progenitor marker expression profile, suggesting evolutionary conservation among lizards.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C121 are supported by observations in this study and cited literature (C118). C119 represents established knowledge. C120 is speculative ('might constitute') but reasonable. C121 is supported by comparison of marker expression data with leopard gecko studies and is appropriately illustrated in Figure 7.

results.result: The DL population is likely strictly necessary for tooth replacement, as it is not detected in monophyodont bearded dragon teeth. The altered proliferation pattern and gene expression differences in acrodont SDL suggest a key role for the DL population in complex SDL organization required for tooth replacement initiation. The maintained OE population in the whole dentition contributes to SDL maintenance and growth, a process not causatively associated with tooth replacement initiation. The comparative analysis indicates the importance of SDL patterning (in addition to maintenance) for vertebrate tooth replacement, involving directional growth, gene expression levels, dynamics, and regionalization. The two separate stem/progenitor populations reveal a new vertebrate dental regenerative strategy associated with cell migration and functional specialization.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C126 represent the major conclusions of the study and are supported by the comprehensive dataset including BrdU pulse-chase, marker expression, DiI labeling, OE removal experiments, and transcriptomics. The inference about DL population necessity (C122) is logical given its absence in non-replacing teeth. The conclusions about SDL patterning (C125) and the novel regenerative strategy (C126) are well-supported by the totality of evidence presented.

results.result: Background claims about vertebrate tooth replacement: Polyphyodonty is the ancestral solution to tooth wear; mammals show reduced tooth generations with most being diphyodont; mice are monophyodont. Tooth replacement generally depends on the dental lamina (DL), which emerges from oral epithelium and is maintained in polyphyodont species to form the successional dental lamina (SDL). In monophyodont/diphyodont species, DL and SDL degenerate rapidly. The DL is considered the main source of putative odontogenic stem cells, with label-retaining cells mapped to various locations in different species (leopard gecko DL, alligator DL bulge, shark SDL/OE, pufferfish superficial DL). The canonical Wnt pathway is a strong candidate for tooth replacement regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C19 represent established knowledge from the literature and are appropriately cited throughout. These background claims provide context for the current study and are well-supported by the cited references. They are not novel findings of this study but rather establish the scientific foundation.

results.result: Background on stem/progenitor markers: Notch signaling regulates stem/progenitor activity in several tissues and is required for tooth morphogenesis and maintenance of murine incisor stem cells. SOX2 is a validated dental progenitor marker in several vertebrate species. Hair follicle stem cell markers LGR5 and IGFBP5 co-localize with LRCs in leopard gecko DL.
results.evaluation: Claims C37, C60, C61 represent established knowledge from cited literature and provide context for the marker analysis performed in this study. These are appropriately cited and support the rationale for marker selection in the experiments.
